2010: Feeling sad, irritable, anxious or tired in a difficult situation is often an expected reaction – not a clinical problem. Labelling too quickly (“it’s depression”, “it’s anxiety”) stigmatises and distracts from what helps in the moment: presence, listening and practical support. What distinguishes a normal reaction from a warning sign is the pattern – frequency, intensity, duration and impact on functioning.
2012: What you feel (as a leader) when dealing with an employee – discomfort, persistent worry, a wish to avoid the conversation – is also information. It is often a first sign that something has changed. Use it to get closer and observe better, never as a diagnosis. If you are left with the feeling that you should ask, you probably already have a reason to do so.

2060: <small style="display:block;font-size:0.9063rem;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--red)">Case study 1</small>An employee with a consistent track record starts missing deadlines and is frequently distracted.
2061: How can the leader step in?
2062: Initial approach: the leader starts a fact-based conversation, using phrases such as: “I’ve noticed some recent difficulty in meeting deadlines and I wanted to understand how you are.”
2063: Exploration: lets the employee explain the context (e.g. overload, personal matters, difficulty concentrating).
2064: Practical adjustments, depending on the situation: reprioritise tasks; temporarily reduce the workload; break complex tasks into stages; clarify objectives.
2065: Defining a plan: set realistic short-term goals; agree follow-up points.
2066: Follow-up: reassess progress after a few days/weeks.
2067: <small style="display:block;font-size:0.9063rem;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--red)">Case study 2</small>An employee reacts disproportionately to feedback and is irritable.
2068: Structured approach: “I noticed that in our last few interactions you’ve been reacting quite intensely. I’d like to understand what’s going on.”
2069: Validation: acknowledge that there may be underlying factors (stress, frustration, overload).
2070: Clarifying limits: separate emotion from behaviour, for example: “I understand you’re under pressure, but we need to ensure a respectful environment in the team.”
2071: Exploring needs: identify sources of stress; adjust workload or expectations, if necessary.
2072: Strategies: suggest breaks; encourage moments of self-regulation before responding.
2073: Monitoring: follow progress and reinforce adjusted behaviour.
2074: <small style="display:block;font-size:0.9063rem;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--red)">Case study 3</small>An employee works excessively, avoids breaks and shows clear signs of exhaustion.
2075: Identification and validation: “I’ve noticed you’ve taken on a very heavy workload and you seem tired to me.”
2076: Normalisation: confirm that overload has an impact and is not sustainable.
2077: Organisational intervention: redistribute tasks; set limits on working hours; encourage real breaks; review priorities.
2078: Reinforcing culture: convey that productivity should not come at the expense of wellbeing.
2080: Ongoing follow-up: monitor signs of recovery or deterioration.
2081: <small style="display:block;font-size:0.9063rem;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--red)">Case study 4</small>An employee significantly reduces interaction with the team and seems distant.
2082: Careful approach: “I’ve sensed you’ve been more distant from the team lately and I wanted to understand how you are.”
2083: Creating a safe space: let the person speak at their own pace, without pressure.
2084: Exploration: identify whether it is demotivation, a personal difficulty or a conflict in the team.
2085: Intervention: facilitate gradual reintegration; promote safe interactions (e.g. smaller meetings); adjust social expectations.
2086: Ongoing support: reinforce availability and keep in regular contact.
